doc.title: Derrick Gardner interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 9, 2013

title: Joe Wilder and Irv Stokes: older trumpeters who play modern
summary: Gardner praises Joe Wilder's versatility and tells of Irv Stokes unexpectedly playing modern at a Hamburg jam session during Black and Blue.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Well said. I’m just going to take a crack and run a few names by you. Joe Wilder?

Oh wow, wow. Probably one of the most consummate trumpet players to ever live. And one of the most versatile trumpeters as well. Not only in jazz but also in classical music. And versatile to the point where he’s able to accept a gig within the classical circle. He’s played — he was one of the first trumpeters to — I won’t say one of the first black trumpeters to play in this — but he was one of the first black trumpeters to choose to play on Broadway, back during the time when there was plenty of work to go around in other jazz circles. He was playing Broadway gigs in the pit orchestras. And such a fabulous style of playing as well. He is able to — he plays, and I’m very careful with trumpeters or musicians of his generation. Because you think that they play in just the older style of improvisation, they play in more of the swing style you know, of improvisation of jazz. But if you had him play on something like “Footprints” or “ESP” or something like that, he will throw something out at you that he played thirty, forty years ago, that fits. And you’ll just be like whoa, where did that come from? This happened to me — well I learned this from my father. My father is another trumpeter that I respect hugely. And I always say that I put my trumpet in the case when he plays. You know, I get out the pad and pencil and take notes. I discovered Clifford Brown through him. That was his man, Clifford Brown. But I was playing a Broadway show that went to Europe. It is called “Black and Blue.” And we were in Germany. We were in Hamburg I believe. And Monday nights is the dark night for Broadway shows, there’s no show on Monday night. So we found a little place in town where we could play on Monday nights. And it was a place called the Dennis Swing Club I think. I think it’s since closed now. But we were playing there on a Monday night and the cat who was playing second trumpet to me, his name was Irv Stokes.

Irv Stokes. You might recognize that name. He played a lot with Lou Donaldson. And a fabulous trumpet player of that older generation. And I’d always played a lot of swing gigs with him you know. And he would just nail it to the wall. So we got to the jam session on Monday night and we were getting all modern playing “Footprints” and “Giant Steps” and all of this stuff, and all of these tunes, uptempo, and stuff like “Just in Time” and what’s another tune like proving ground tunes —

“Cherokee.” And he comes in and he gets up and plays and he just falls right in. And then we played something like — I think we played “Footprints.” And he just switched like a light bulb and started playing this other way and everything he played just fit right into the chord changes, right into the vibe of the tune, and we were all like whoa, where did this side of Irv come from? We didn’t know he even played like this. And the whole time © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -14-
he was playing I had my note pad and I would say oh, oh really, oh wow. So I learned. So okay Sonny boy, in class today we are going to learn this.
